```{r rl-setup, echo=FALSE}
# From week 3's setup chunk: the colors and the math-label helper these figures use.
# Put these lines in the notes' setup chunk (drop what the notes already define).
# cividis: viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)]
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two

# Labels with math letters. In `label`, the text between dollar signs is drawn in
# MathJax_Math, the TeX italic of an older MathJax, which looks like the italic of the
# slides' formulas; the rest is drawn in the device's default font. The pieces are placed
# when the plot is drawn, so they stay together at any figure size. A label cannot hold a
# literal dollar sign, and hjust and vjust are numbers. `nudge_y` moves the labels up by
# that many points (y = Inf is the top of the panel).
GeomMathText <- ggproto("GeomMathText", Geom,
  required_aes = c("x", "y", "label"),
  default_aes = aes(colour = "black", size = 6, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
  draw_key = draw_key_text,
  draw_panel = function(data, panel_params, coord, nudge_y = 0) {
    data <- coord$transform(data, panel_params)
    labels <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(data)), function(i) {
      d <- data[i, ]
      parts <- strsplit(as.character(d$label), "$", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
      math <- seq_along(parts) %% 2 == 0
      keep <- nzchar(parts)
      if (!any(keep)) return(grid::nullGrob())
      # math pieces also ask for italic, so that they stay italic if the font is missing
      font <- function(m) grid::gpar(col = d$colour, fontsize = d$size * .pt,
                                     fontfamily = if (m) "MathJax_Math" else "",
                                     fontface = if (m) "italic" else "plain")
      pieces <- unname(Map(function(p, m) grid::textGrob(p, gp = font(m)), parts[keep], math[keep]))
      widths <- lapply(pieces, grid::grobWidth)
      x <- unit(d$x, "native") - d$hjust * Reduce(`+`, widths)
      # one baseline for all the pieces, placed by the height of the default font's capitals
      y <- unit(d$y, "native") + unit(nudge_y, "pt") -
        d$vjust * grid::grobHeight(grid::textGrob("M", gp = font(FALSE)))
      for (k in seq_along(pieces)) {
        pieces[[k]] <- grid::editGrob(pieces[[k]], x = x, y = y, just = c("left", "bottom"))
        x <- x + widths[[k]]
      }
      grid::gTree(children = do.call(grid::gList, pieces))
    })
    grid::gTree(children = do.call(grid::gList, labels))
  }
)
geom_mathtext <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, ...) {
  layer(geom = GeomMathText, mapping = mapping, data = data, stat = "identity",
        position = "identity", show.legend = FALSE, inherit.aes = FALSE, params = list(...))
}
# The math letters and pi in the figures are drawn in MathJax_Math. Stop if it is missing,
# rather than draw them in another font without saying so.
if (requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
    !"MathJax_Math" %in% systemfonts::system_fonts()$family) {
  stop("The font MathJax_Math is not installed. It draws the math letters in this file's ",
       "figures (on Debian or Ubuntu: apt-get install fonts-mathjax).")
}
```

## Reinforcement learning

**Notation:** this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning:
$S$ state, $A$ action, $R$ reward, $\pi$ policy, $U$ utility.

An agent observes a **state** $S$, takes an **action** $A$, and receives
a **reward** $R$. A **policy** $\pi$ is a rule that chooses the action
from the state, $A = \pi(S)$, and learning means changing the policy to
make the expected reward, $E_\pi[R]$, large, where $E_\pi$ is the
expectation when the agent acts by $\pi$. The **utility** $U$ is what
we care about. A utilitarian would choose the policy whose
expected utility $E_\pi[U]$ is largest. The agent is given $R$ instead,
because $R$ can be measured and $U$ often cannot: in the job center
below, $U$ needs what would have happened without the course. $R$ and
$U$ can come apart.

```{r rl_loop, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.7, fig.width=6, dev.args=list(symbolfamily=grDevices::cairoSymbolFont("MathJax_Math", usePUA=FALSE)), fig.alt="A loop: the agent, with policy pi, sends an action A to the environment, which returns a state S and a reward R to the agent."}
# dev.args draws pi in MathJax_Math, the TeX italic of an older MathJax, so that it looks
# like the pi in the formulas. Where that font is missing, the system substitutes another.
loop_boxes <- data.frame(x = c(0, 3), y = c(0, 0), label = c("atop(agent, policy~pi)", "environment"))
loop_top <- data.frame(x = 0.62, y = 0.28, xend = 2.28, yend = 0.28)
loop_bottom <- data.frame(x = 2.28, y = -0.28, xend = 0.62, yend = -0.28)
loop_text <- data.frame(x = c(1.45, 1.45), y = c(1.12, -1.12),
                        label = c("action $A$", "state $S$, reward $R$"))
ggplot() +
  geom_curve(data = loop_top, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend), curvature = -0.35,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_curve(data = loop_bottom, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend), curvature = -0.35,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(data = loop_boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 4.5,
             label.padding = unit(0.5, "lines")) +
  geom_mathtext(data = loop_text, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4.2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.9, 3.9), ylim = c(-1.3, 1.3)) +
  theme_void()
```

Amodei and colleagues (2016) use a cleaning robot as a running example.
In these letters, the state is what the robot's camera shows, the
actions are where to move and whether to clean, and the utility is a
clean room. If the reward is for not seeing any mess, the robot can
earn it by closing its eyes, or by covering the mess with something it
cannot see through.

```{r robot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.3, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Three rooms, each earning reward 1. Left: the robot cleans, and its view shows no mess. Middle: it closes its eyes, and the mess stays. Right: it covers the mess, which stays under the cover."}
panels <- c("cleans", "closes its eyes", "covers the mess")
room <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels))
cone <- do.call(rbind, lapply(panels[c(1, 3)], function(p)
  data.frame(panel = p, x = c(2.6, 9.6, 9.6), y = c(2.3, 7.4, 3.0))))
mess <- data.frame(panel = rep(panels[2:3], each = 2), x = c(7.6, 8.4, 7.6, 8.4), y = c(5.0, 4.3, 5.0, 4.3))
cover <- data.frame(panel = panels[3], xmin = 6.5, xmax = 9.7, ymin = 3.2, ymax = 6.1)
caption <- data.frame(panel = panels, x = 5, y = -1.6,
                      label = c("$R$ = 1, room clean", "$R$ = 1, room dirty", "$R$ = 1, room dirty"))
for (d in c("cone", "mess", "cover", "caption")) {
  z <- get(d); z$panel <- factor(z$panel, levels = panels); assign(d, z)
}
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = room, aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0, ymax = 8), fill = NA, color = slate, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_polygon(data = cone, aes(x, y), fill = gold, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = mess, aes(x, y), size = 5, color = khaki) +
  geom_rect(data = cover, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = cgray, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x = 2, y = 2), aes(x, y), size = 6, color = navy) +
  geom_mathtext(data = caption, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.3, 10.3), ylim = c(-2.4, 8.3)) +
  theme_void() + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11), panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

Now a variant of the job center, with 100 places on the course, which
helps some people more than others. Of people who worked last year, 70% are in work six months
later if they take the course and 64% if they do not; of people who did
not work last year, 40% and 14%. The state is a person's record, the
action is to refer or not, and the center is judged on the share of
the people it refers who are in work, its placement rate. That rate is
its reward. Referring 100 people who worked last year earns a rate of
70% and puts 6 more people in work, on average, than would be in work
without the course. Referring 100 who did not earns 40% and puts 26 more
in work. A center judged on its placement rate refers the first group;
a utilitarian counting the jobs the course creates refers the second,
and so serves the people who need the course most.

```{r skim, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.2, fig.width=6, fig.alt="Two panels of invented numbers for the variant job center. Placement rate: 70 percent if it sends people who worked last year, 40 percent if it sends those who did not. Extra people in work: 6 against 26."}
skim <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(c("worked last year", "did not"), 2), levels = c("worked last year", "did not")),
                   panel = factor(rep(c("R", "U"), each = 2), levels = c("R", "U")),
                   value = c(70, 40, 6, 26), shown = c("70%", "40%", "6", "26"))
# the panels' titles, drawn above the panels by geom_mathtext so that R and U are in the
# formulas' italic (a strip's text has one font)
titles <- data.frame(panel = factor(c("R", "U"), levels = c("R", "U")), x = 1.5, y = Inf,
                     label = c("$R$: placement rate", "$U$: extra people in work"))
ggplot(skim, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = shown), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  geom_mathtext(data = titles, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 8.8 / .pt, colour = "grey10",
                vjust = 0, nudge_y = 4.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = two) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "the 100 people sent", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(t = 18, r = 5.5, b = 5.5, l = 5.5))
```

Choosing people who would have done well anyway is called cream
skimming. Heckman, Heinrich and Smith (2002) studied it in US
job-training centers funded under the Job Training Partnership Act,
which were judged partly on employment rates. They found the short-run
measures "weakly, and sometimes perversely, related to long run
impacts." They also found that cream skimming made little difference
to the programs' efficiency, in either direction, unlike the invented
numbers above, and concluded: "Opposition to cream skimming must come
on equity grounds." Equity here is about who is served; efficiency is
about the total.

Each of the four difficulties of utilitarianism becomes a choice
someone makes in building such an agent. Defining utility becomes
choosing $R$, a measurable stand-in for $U$, and in both examples the
two come apart. Trading off between people becomes adding the reward up
over the people the agent serves; the placement rate counts only the
people referred. Judging acts or rules becomes choosing a policy, a
rule that treats alike everyone in the same state. Judging each action
on its own and judging the rule can give different answers: when a rule
has to treat different situations alike, as a model that sees only a
few variables about each person does; when places are limited, so that
one referral uses a place another person could have had; and when
people respond to the rule itself. Predicting consequences becomes
choosing a model of what the actions do, which is a causal model.

Is $E_\pi[U]$ a causal quantity? It can be read as one, the expected
utility if the agent's actions were set by $\pi$, but that reading
needs assumptions beyond this week's. An intervention in this week's
sense sets a variable for everyone in a population. Here one agent
follows a rule. The people and systems it acts on may respond to what
it does, sometimes adversarially, and what happens to one of them can
depend on what was done to others. Causal reinforcement learning, a
subfield surveyed by Deng, Jiang, Long and Zhang (2023), brings causal
models into reinforcement learning.

These letters clash with the ones used for prediction, which most of
the course uses.

| | prediction | reinforcement learning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ | sensitive attribute: something a person *is* | action: something an agent *does* |
| $R$ | risk score, with $\hat Y = 1\{R \ge t\}$ | reward |
| $U$ | unobserved variable | utility |
| $S$, $\pi$ | not used | state, policy |

If you read about reinforcement learning you will meet these letters
with these meanings. New letters invented for this course would teach a
convention nobody else uses. Two rules are enough. Material that uses
the reinforcement-learning letters says so in one line at the top, as
this section does. And the two sets of letters are never mixed inside
one diagram or one derivation. A classifier described as an agent takes
its prediction $\hat Y$ as its action, which reinforcement learning
would write as $A$. Mixing the two there would give $A$ two meanings in
one line.
